thread.title: 'Siri, how healthy am I?' MedStar among the first to test Apple’s health records feature.

author: Tina Reed
title: 'Siri, how healthy am I?' MedStar among the first to test Apple’s health records feature.
text: – Staff Reporter, Washington Business Journal Jan 25, 2018, 2:46pm EST With the iPhone's Health app, you can already count your steps, track your sleep and even mind the number of minutes you've been mindful. Now, Apple has posted an update to allow users to pull up their electronic medical records. MedStar Health is one of 12 medical institutions across the country collaborating with Apple Inc . (NASDAQ: AAPL) on a feature, which allows users to view parts of their medical records in their Health app on their iPhone. The Cupertino, California-based tech giant just released the update to a dozen health providers that are customers of three major electronic health records vendors, including Epic Corp., athenahealth Inc. (NASDAQ: ATHN) and Cerner Corp. (NASDAQ: CERN), which is MedStar's vendor. In a few days, that Health app update will be available for consumers — including MedStar's patients — to sign up for a public beta and connect to their electronic records from their iPhones. Columbia-based MedStar declined to comment on specifics of the beta test. But it said, generally, putting data in the hands of consumers is a way to improve the patient experience. The system operates MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, MedStar Washington Hospital Center and MedStar Montgomery Medical Center, as well as several outpatient clinics throughout the region. “Giving consumers easy access to their personal health data whenever and wherever they access health care services is not only personally empowering — it will make for better health care," said Dr. Stephen Evans , MedStar’s executive vice president for medical affairs and chief medical officer, in an emailed statement. In addition to MedStar, Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore is also testing the app. Other participants include Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles; Penn Medicine In Philadelphia; Geisinger Health System in Danville, Pennsylvania; U.C. San Diego Health System in San Diego; and Rush University Medical Center in Chicago. Apple officials said they expect to add more hospitals and electronic health records systems to access the iPhone feature in coming months. But they declined to give an interview for further details. “Our goal is to help consumers live a better day. We’ve worked closely with the health community to create an experience everyone has wanted for years — to view medical records easily and securely right on your iPhone,” said Jeff Williams , Apple’s chief operating officer, in a public statement. “By empowering customers to see their overall health, we hope to help consumers better understand their health and help them lead healthier lives.”
